blocks.x: Okay, we're going.
Well, this is Robert Lewis. I've come down to New Orleans to visit Bill Russell.
I understand you were one of the two pupils that Sidney Bechet had, and I hope you could tell us a little bit about your lessons with him and your experiences with Sidney.

Well, I guess I was one of his pupils, but not for very long. I was going to school at the time, and of course he was traveling a great deal. And I suppose I took no more than eight lessons in total from him.
What year was that about?
Well, I started in 1947.
What did he teach you? The very first lesson, what did he have you to do?
Well, he asked me to play something on the clarinet, and I played it very badly, of course. So then I came back, and he gave me a lesson.

You mentioned it was a little piece that you'd heard from a Johnny Dodds record. Oh, yeah, Stealing Away. Well, I think of it. You mentioned this afternoon that he didn't think too much of Johnny Dodds. Was that his musicianship, or what did he say?
Well, Sidney was always Sidney, and when it came to talking about other musicians, why, of course, he had to think about himself too, the way many musicians do.
Yeah. Did he make any remarks, especially if you remember, about Dodds? Why didn't he like him so well? Maybe he couldn't read what he thought so well, or what?
Well, he just didn't think he was the musician that Sidney Vichay was. Yeah.
Well, Dodds would have said that too.
Well, I'm sure of that too, yeah.
All right, good back to your lesson now. What piece did he teach you first?
Well, it was a little exercise in the key of F. Shall I?
Yeah, in the low register. Did he have you to stick to the low register first?
Yeah, that's right, and it was mostly training in fifths and thirds.
One other thing before we start, in case I forget it. Did he use the double embouchure or the single embouchure? Did he bite the...
No, he always used a single embouchure.
Put his teeth under the mouth.
Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Okay.
All right. Let's see what we can do. See if I can still remember it.
Did he teach you that by ear?
Oh, yes, all by ear.
All the time that you studied with him, it was always by ear.
Everything we did was by ear.
He never wrote down anything for you or had you bring any rhythm music?

No, no. Once he asked me to tell me which keys were which, and I put my finger on A, and I called it B, and he didn't call me on it, so I thought I'd get away with that. But we didn't go into the technical aspects very deeply.
Did he ever talk anything about breathing or explaining about a vibrato, for instance?
No, he said to leave the vibrato alone. He said that's something that you can do by yourself if you want to or leave it alone if you want to.
I was going to ask, one time you say you had sort of a bad lesson, and what was the remark he made to you? You told me this afternoon something you wouldn't talk to him that way, or what was it?

Oh, yes. I came in. I hadn't prepared a lesson at all, and I thought I could sort of get by with it. Well, not with Sidney. He said, would you talk to me that way? I just let go with some terrible squawks, and that's what he said. Would you talk to me that way?
That reminds me of the other occasion you told me in Belgium once when he didn't like this drummer. You can tell that little story there, too, if you like.
Oh, yes.
How he growl, I think.

Yeah, the drummer wasn't doing what he should have done, and Sidney, first of all, started stomping one foot on the stage platform to get him in time, and the drummer still didn't get the idea, so Sidney took the entire band, that's the walking band, around to the backside of the stage, which was open. Well, that's where the drummer was, and when Sidney got there, he growled furiously. I think the drummer came, too, eventually.

I was interested, because other New Orleans musicians I know, too, consider music sort of a form of communication, which it really is, and they'll talk. I think that fight between Ed Garland and Ed and Ori, Kid Ori, out in San Francisco, when Garland knocked him off the stand is when Ori said something to him on the trombone, a few dirty words or something, and made Garland mad.
Well, it's a very expressive form of music.

Yeah, that's right. I was going to ask about a saxophone. We had that letter that you were kind enough to let us copy this afternoon when he gave you the saxophone. That was about two years ago, you say?
Yes, that's right.
Almost two years before he died, then, too, or a year and a half.
Yeah.
What make is it?
It's a busher.
Just a straight model. Was his ever gold, and you have it gold-plated, I notice now.
It was. It was originally gold-plated. The repairman told me it had been gold-plated. Of course, there wasn't much gold left on it. When I got it, Sidney had left it in this country for some time.
Do you want to play a few notes, just so we can see where you have Sidney's sax here?
All right.
Thank you.
